title: The Printing Press: History's First Viral Moment
subtitle: One machine dropped the cost of copying an idea by orders of magnitude — and toppled churches, sparked science, and remade Europe.
hook: Before ~1440, a book was copied by hand — months of a monk's labour for one copy. Then Gutenberg combined movable type with a wine press, and suddenly you could print hundreds of identical pages a day. The cost of copying an idea collapsed. What followed — the Reformation, the Scientific Revolution, mass literacy — is what happens when information suddenly gets cheap. Today: humanity's first taste of things going viral.

sections.heading: Cheap copies change everything
sections.body: The press didn't just make books faster — it changed *who* could have ideas and how fast they spread. When copying is expensive, knowledge stays locked with a tiny elite (remember the scribe class from the writing lesson). When copying is cheap, ideas escape. A pamphlet could reach thousands in weeks; a challenge to authority could outrun any attempt to suppress it.

sections.caption: The press collapsed the cost of copying — and cheap copies let ideas escape the elite and spread faster than authorities could contain them.

sections.label: It broke a monopoly on truth
sections.body: Luther's 95 Theses went 'viral' in 1517 — printed, translated, and spread across Germany in weeks, something impossible a century earlier. The Catholic Church could not un-print them. For the first time, an institution's monopoly on which ideas circulated was broken by a machine. Every information technology since has re-run this fight between gatekeepers and cheap copying.

sections.label: Cheap ideas aren't always true ideas
sections.body: The press spread science *and* witch-hunting manuals and propaganda. Lowering the cost of copying amplifies whatever spreads — good and bad alike. If that sounds like the internet and social media, it should: same mechanism, new century. Cheap distribution is power, not virtue.

sections.caption: How Gutenberg's press changed the world.

takeaways: The press (~1440) collapsed the **cost of copying** an idea.
Cheap copies let knowledge **escape the elite** and spread fast.
It fueled the **Reformation, Scientific Revolution, and mass literacy**.
It **broke institutional monopolies** on which ideas could circulate (Luther went 'viral').
Cheap distribution amplifies **good and bad** alike — the same dynamic as today's internet.

quiz.q: What did the printing press fundamentally change?
options: The cost of copying/spreading ideas — collapsing it
quiz.explain: Cheap copying is the lever behind every downstream change.

quiz.q: Why did the press threaten established authorities?
options: Ideas could now spread faster than they could be suppressed, breaking their monopoly on information
quiz.explain: Luther's Theses spreading in weeks is the classic example — un-suppressable.

quiz.q: CALLBACK: How does this extend the writing lesson (Day 3)?
options: Writing let knowledge be stored & copied; the press made copying so cheap that ideas escaped the elite entirely — the same info-technology arc, scaled up
quiz.explain: Store → transmit → accumulate, now at industrial scale. Each info technology re-runs the fight between gatekeepers and cheap copying.

tg_quiz.q: The printing press's core effect was to collapse the cost of…
tg_quiz.correct: Right — cheap copies let ideas escape the elite.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's the cost of copying ideas — that's what changed everything.
tg_quiz.explain: Cheap distribution → Reformation, science, mass literacy.
